query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, local chemical clustering driven by strongly negative mixing enthalpies (especially between Al and Ni and by the self-affinity of Al) in the context of high configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion governs phase stability by stabilizing a single-phase or weakly ordered solid solution that resists the formation of brittle secondary phases under high temperature, irradiation, and cryogenic loading.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic or near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy (e.g., Al0.1CrCoFeNi) that under standard processing forms a single-phase face-centered cubic (fcc) or disordered solid solution with evidence for atomic-scale clustering (notably Al–Al and Al–Ni clusters).
generation.intervention: A controlled experiment comparing alloys with low Al content versus alloys with relatively high Al content while applying treatments such as high-temperature annealing, ion irradiation, and compressive mechanical loading.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under high-temperature conditions to assess thermal stability, under ion irradiation to simulate displacement cascades for evaluating precipitation resistance, and under compressive mechanical deformation at cryogenic temperatures to probe clustering-to-ordering transitions.
generation.structural_mediator: The local atomic-scale chemical clustering and short-range order, especially among Al–Al and Al–Ni pairs, that modulates the nucleation of ordered domains versus phase separation.
generation.mechanism: Strong, negative mixing enthalpies between certain element pairs (especially Al–Ni and Al–Al) drive local clustering within a high configurational entropy matrix, which operates via diffusion-controlled kinetics by reducing atomic mobility and suppressing diffusion-driven phase separation under thermal or irradiation conditions; under compressive or cryogenic deformation, slight atomic rearrangements induce a controlled clustering-to-ordering transition that enhances work hardening and strength without compromising toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under the specified treatments, the low-Al (≈0.1) alloy will show a persistent single-phase (or weakly ordered) structure with clear evidence of local Al-centered clusters and no formation of brittle secondary phases. It will also exhibit improved high-temperature strength, better radiation tolerance (with suppressed precipitation), and maintain high cryogenic ductility, relative to high-Al alloys that tend to form multiphase microstructures (e.g., including sigma phases).
generation.baseline: Alloys with higher Al contents (e.g., Al ≈1.5) that, under similar processing conditions, develop multiphase microstructures (such as BCC or sigma phases) leading to diminished environmental resistance, increased brittleness under cryogenic conditions, and reduced irradiation tolerance.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni compositions near equiatomic ratios or with low Al additions (typically within a narrow Al mole fraction range where a single-phase solid solution is achievable). Deviations far outside this compositional window (e.g., very high Al content) or processing conditions that exceed the tested temperature/irradiation ranges may not follow the same clustering‐driven mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative relationship between the extent of local clustering and the precise improvements in mechanical and environmental properties is not fully defined. The exact Al-content threshold and the role of other alloying elements in modulating the clustering behavior require further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA specimens: one with low Al content (e.g., Al0.1CrCoFeNi) and another with high Al content (e.g., Al1.5CrCoFeNi). Subject both sets to identical high-temperature annealing, ion irradiation, and compressive deformation (including tests at cryogenic temperatures) while characterizing the microstructure using X-ray diffraction, TEM, and atom-probe tomography. Concurrently, measure mechanical properties (tensile strength, ductility, fracture toughness) and assess the formation or suppression of secondary phases.
measurements: Phase identification (XRD, TEM) to detect fcc/diffuse ordered versus multiphase (BCC/sigma) structures
Atomistic-scale chemical clustering analysis (atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM)
Mechanical testing under defined thermal and cryogenic conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the low-Al (≈0.1) alloy does not show enhanced phase stability (i.e., if it forms secondary brittle phases or does not exhibit a clustering-to-ordering transition under compressive strain) and its mechanical/environmental properties are no better than or comparable to those of the high-Al alloy, then the proposed mechanism is falsified. Similarly, if evidence of local chemical clustering is absent or not correlated with improved performance, the hypothesis must be rejected.

In contrast, the configurational entropy of single phase HEA Al0.1CoCrFeNi is much higher, which competes with the positive mixing enthalpy in the ion irradiation and reduces the thermodynamic driving force for precipitation. Furthermore, due to the high configurational entropy the thermodynamic stability of single phase Al0.1CoCrFeNi is increased with temperature increasing, enhancing the stability of random solid solution during the evolution of high energy displacement cascades induced by ion irradiation. Another reason for the great resistance of single phase HEA to precipitation may be the sluggish atomic diffusion. The formation of precipitates in the ion irradiation is attributed to the fluxes of irradiation-induced defects, the defect fluxes towards various sinks result in the solute depletion or segregation at sinks.
